text: AI agent failures often start with authority that is broader than the job. Audit what the agent may read, decide, execute and escalate before production.
An agent contract should answer four questions before deployment: what it may access, what it may execute, where human approval is required, and what evidence proves completion.
The risky gap in agent systems is often not model quality. It is permission design. Narrow the authority surface, define stop conditions, and verify the handoff before scaling.
Before adding another AI tool, map overlap, ownership, human review and break-even. Start with the self-service decision layer, then escalate only if the stack is messy.
AI spend gets expensive when tools overlap and nobody owns the workflow. Put every tool against one measurable job, one owner and one keep-or-cut threshold.
A useful software review ends with a decision, not a prettier inventory. KEEP, REDUCE, CONSOLIDATE, REVIEW or CANCEL should be tied to workflow value and cost.
Agent tooling changes fast. Brain, Policy, Skills and State should stay portable. Cross-Agent Operating Kit packages that operating layer with human and cost gates.
If changing agent runtimes means rebuilding policy, state and skills from scratch, the operating layer is too coupled. Portability should be designed before migration hurts.
A durable agent stack separates the model from the operating contract: policy, skills, state, human gates and cost limits. Then tools can change without losing control.
